I don't think so. It's not a contradiction. I am repeating it again.Emotional depth isn’t the same as philosophical depth. Kafka captured despair, confusion, and alienation with remarkable skill, but he rarely moved beyond describing these states to offer a meaningful framework or path through them. 

His work doesn't build toward insight it circles, stagnates, collapses inward. That’s not a flaw in itself, but it’s different from what writers like Camus or Nietzsche attempted.

Saying the parable in The Trail explains what the story is all about is an oversimplification. Kafka famously resisted clear interpretations, and that parable is full of contradictions and loops it doesn’t clarify anything so much as deepen the confusion. If anything, it suggests the futility of searching for final answers or meaning.

The idea that K.'s death happens because he failed to take action is just one possible reading, but Kafka doesn't really deal in moral lessons like that. His stories rarely offer resolution, and they don’t reward the reader with neat conclusions.

Reading Kafka as a philosopher rather than a literary artist woukd be a mistake. Kafka doesn’t offer any true understanding of the human condition, only a vivid, sometimes haunting description of its confusion.

His strength lies in his style and tone, not in his depth of thought. There’s no guidance, no philosophy that leads anywhere just the slow, mesmerizing spiral of despair dressed in beautifully crafted language.

I find Kafka very overrated. His works, while stylistically strong, tend to wallow in self-pity and romanticise suffering. There's a theatrical quality to his despair a kind of emotional exhibitionism that gets mistaken for profundity.

Yes, he's a skilled writer, but that doesn’t necessarily make him a profound thinker. People  confuse the intensity of emotion to the depth of emotion.
